title: How does your brain decide what to remember?

cards.title: Odds are, you never lost that memory. You never made it.
cards.text: Ever forgotten where you put your keys? Odds are, you never really “lost” that memory. You never made it. Making a memory starts with encoding: turning what you see and hear into a form your brain can keep.

notes: Keys put down while your mind is elsewhere
What you see and hear goes into the brain as a memory: encoding

cards.title: Attention works like a spotlight on what you take in
cards.text: Your senses take in far more than you could ever keep, so attention works like a spotlight. Only what it lands on gets a chance to become a memory. The rest mostly fades.

notes: Many things pour in through the senses
A spotlight lands on one; the rest fade

cards.title: What you noticed waits in a tiny workspace
cards.text: What you noticed then waits in working memory, a tiny workspace that holds about four things. Once your mind moves on, they slip away in seconds, unless you work with them.

notes: A small tray holds about four things
When the mind moves on, they slip away

cards.title: How you work with it decides how well it sticks
cards.text: And how you work with them decides how well they stick. Just repeating a phone number leaves a weak memory. Thinking about what something means, and linking it to what you know, leaves a strong one.

notes: Repeating: a faint memory with one thin link
Meaning and links to what you know: a strong memory with many links

cards.title: You've seen thousands of pennies but never really looked
cards.text: You can picture a penny, but could you draw which way the head faces, or where the words sit? Most people can't: they've seen thousands but never really looked.
cards.takeaway: You can't remember what you never took in.

notes: A blurry penny: which way does the head face, where are the words?
Many pennies seen, none looked at
